hints: Differentiate \(x=3-\cos2\theta\) and \(y=2\theta+\sin2\theta\), applying the chain rule to each double angle.
In the resulting quotient, use \(1+\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta\) and \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), then cancel common factors.
walkthrough:
State the given parametric equations of the curve for $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$:
$$x = 3 - \cos 2\theta, \quad y = 2\theta + \sin 2\theta$$

Differentiate $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dx}{d\theta} = \dfrac{d}{d\theta}(3 - \cos 2\theta) = 0 - (-\sin 2\theta)(2) = 2\sin 2\theta$$

Differentiate $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = \dfrac{d}{d\theta}(2\theta + \sin 2\theta) = 2 + (\cos 2\theta)(2) = 2 + 2\cos 2\theta = 2(1 + \cos 2\theta)$$

Recall the double-angle trigonometric identities for cosine and sine:
$$\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \implies 1 + \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta$$
$$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$$

Substitute these identities into the expression for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2\cos^2\theta}{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}$$

Divide numerator and denominator by $2\cos\theta$ (which is non-zero since $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$):
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \cot\theta, \quad \text{as required.}$$
